**Proof.**

Consider the conjugation action of $G$ on $N$. Since $N \trianglelefteq G$, conjugation by any $g \in G$ restricts to an automorphism of $N$, giving a homomorphism
$$\varphi \colon G \to \operatorname{Aut}(N), \qquad \varphi(g)(n) = gng^{-1}.$$

**Kernel of $\varphi$.** We have $\ker\varphi = C_G(N) := \{g \in G : gng^{-1}=n \text{ for all } n\in N\}$, the centralizer of $N$ in $G$.

**Image of $\varphi$.** The restriction of $\varphi$ to $N$ is the natural map $N \to \operatorname{Inn}(N)$, whose kernel is $Z(N)$. Since $Z(N)=1$, this restriction is an isomorphism $N \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} \operatorname{Inn}(N)$. Hence
$$\operatorname{Inn}(N) = \varphi(N) \leq \varphi(G) \leq \operatorname{Aut}(N) = \operatorname{Inn}(N),$$
where the last equality is the hypothesis. Therefore $\varphi(G) = \operatorname{Inn}(N) = \varphi(N)$.

**The complement.** Since $\varphi(G)=\varphi(N)$, for every $g\in G$ there exists $n\in N$ with $\varphi(g)=\varphi(n)$, i.e. $gn^{-1}\in\ker\varphi = C_G(N)$. Thus
$$G = N\cdot C_G(N).$$
Moreover,
$$N \cap C_G(N) = Z(N) = 1,$$
since an element of $N$ that centralizes all of $N$ lies in the center of $N$. Therefore $G = N \rtimes C_G(N)$, and setting $H := C_G(N)$, we have $G = NH$ with $N\cap H = 1$; so $H$ is a complement to $N$ in $G$.

**Normality of $H$.** The centralizer of a normal subgroup is itself normal: if $h\in C_G(N)$ and $g\in G$, then for every $n\in N$,
$$(ghg^{-1})\,n\,(ghg^{-1})^{-1} = g\,h\,(g^{-1}ng)\,h^{-1}\,g^{-1}.$$
Since $N\trianglelefteq G$, we have $g^{-1}ng\in N$, and since $h$ centralizes $N$, $h(g^{-1}ng)h^{-1}=g^{-1}ng$. Hence the expression equals $g(g^{-1}ng)g^{-1}=n$, proving $ghg^{-1}\in C_G(N)$. Thus $H=C_G(N)\trianglelefteq G$.

We have shown that $H=C_G(N)$ is a complement to $N$ in $G$ and that $H$ is normal in $G$. $\blacksquare$
